Why would a children's heart surgeon call Ferrari for help?
Picture this. Great Ormond Street Hospital, London.
A baby's just come through heart surgery.
You'd think that's the hard part. It's not.
Now they've got to move that tiny patient to intensive care.
Every tube, wire and monitor comes off... and goes back on.
Several teams round one little bed. Stuff gets missed.
Then two of its doctors studied an F1 pit stop.
Twenty-odd mechanics, one car, done in seconds. Nobody's in anybody's way.
So they did the obvious thing. They called Ferrari.
And Ferrari's crew actually watched videos of the hospital's handovers.
The fix? Straight out of the pit lane.
One person in charge, like the lollipop man.
Everyone's got one job. Same order, every time.
Plus a checklist, so nothing slips through.
And the result?
Technical errors? Down forty-two percent.
Missing information? Nearly halved.
A sport obsessed with tenths of a second taught doctors how to protect what really matters.
So next time someone asks you...
